questions.q: In this lesson's solution design sequence, which step comes before the data model mapping step?
options: Design review
Automation and UI design
The application boundary decision
The quality attribute check
questions.explain: The sequence runs requirements intake, domain modeling, cloud/feature fit check, application boundary decision, then data model mapping -- the boundary decision comes before mapping the domain model into actual objects and fields.

questions.q: What does this lesson say happens when a team skips domain modeling and the cloud/feature fit check, jumping straight from a stakeholder's request to building custom objects?
options: Projects frequently end up custom-building something a standard object already covered
Nothing different happens -- the order of these steps has no real effect
This is actually the recommended fast path for experienced architects
Salesforce automatically blocks custom object creation until domain modeling is documented
questions.explain: Skipping the fit check specifically risks building custom solutions for problems a standard object or feature already solves, which is exactly the failure mode this lesson warns about.

questions.q: Why does this lesson warn against designing automation before the data model is finalized?
options: Because Flow cannot technically be built until a data model exists at all
Because automation design has no dependency on the data model whatsoever
Because this ordering issue only affects Apex, never Flow
Because a Flow built around a field that later gets redesigned is a predictable, specific problem caused by reordering these steps
questions.explain: The lesson gives this as a direct example of what goes wrong from reordering: automation built around a field that the (still-unfinalized) data model later changes out from under it.

questions.q: What does this lesson say is required for a design to be considered 'ready to hand off' to a build team?
options: A verbal agreement reached in a planning meeting is sufficient on its own
A written artifact documenting the sourced requirements, domain model, data model, automation/UI approach with reasoning, and any known quality-attribute trade-offs or debt
Only the final data model needs to be documented; everything else can stay verbal
A design is ready once a single stakeholder approves it verbally, regardless of documentation
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly lists what a design artifact needs to document and states that a verbal-only agreement is an intention, not yet an actual design ready to hand to a build team who wasn't in the room.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the step sequence isn't perfectly rigid in real projects?
options: Because the steps can be done in literally any order with no consequence
Because the sequence only applies to Technical Architect-level projects
Because real projects sometimes loop back -- a later step, like data model mapping, can reveal the domain model from an earlier step was incomplete, requiring iteration
Because design review always happens first, before any other step
questions.explain: The lesson acknowledges real iteration -- a later step can surface a gap in an earlier one, sending the process back -- while still insisting the overall priority order (domain before schema before automation) matters for catching problems cheaply.
